title: India Has Raised Fuel Prices Four Times in Three Weeks. The Oil Minister Says They Will Fall.
excerpt: Hardeep Singh Puri tells CNN-News18 that oil prices 'cannot remain at their current height' for long, that India has 76–80 days of reserves, and that Western Hemisphere suppliers will step in. But he also warns of a 'totally different ball game' if the Iran war drags past March 2027.
body:
Four fuel price hikes in three weeks. Petrol up 7.8 percent. Diesel up 8.6 percent. And on Monday, India's petroleum minister went on national television to tell a country of 1.4 billion people that relief is coming — eventually.

Union Minister Hardeep Singh Puri, speaking to CNN-News18, said India expects both oil and gas prices to drop in the coming months, and that the country has enough strategic reserves to weather the current storm. "Oil prices cannot remain at their current height for a very long time," he said.

The reassurance comes at a moment when Indian consumers are feeling the most sustained energy price pressure since 2022. Global crude has surged 40 percent since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran restricted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, pushing Brent to trade near $97 a barrel on Monday.

## The Numbers Behind the Pain

Before the conflict erupted in February, India sourced more than 40 percent of its crude oil imports and roughly 90 percent of its liquefied petroleum gas — the fuel most Indian households use for cooking — through the Hormuz corridor. That supply line is now effectively choked.

State-owned fuel retailers held off on price increases during state elections earlier this year. But once the electoral calendar cleared, four hikes came in rapid succession since mid-May, ending a period of artificial price stability that had been sustained by oil marketing companies absorbing losses.

Puri said India currently has oil and gas reserves sufficient for 76 to 80 days. "That's comfortable," he added, while acknowledging that the arithmetic changes dramatically if the crisis deepens.

## The Worst-Case Scenario He Named

In a rare moment of official candour, Puri addressed the question of what happens if the Iran war extends well beyond current expectations.

"Recently, someone was discussing what is the worst-case scenario in the Iran war. Supposing the crisis goes on till March 31, 2027," Puri recounted. "I replied: 'Wait a minute, then we are in a totally different ball game. That would be global depression.'"

It was a striking admission from a sitting cabinet minister — not a prediction, but an acknowledgement of the catastrophic tail risk that Indian policymakers are privately modeling.

## The Diversification Play

Puri expressed confidence that India's diversification efforts are working. He specifically named the UAE as a reliable alternative supplier, noting that Abu Dhabi had offered LPG cargoes directly to India — a sign of the diplomatic capital New Delhi has been spending to keep energy flowing.

"We are very fortunate to have friends like the UAE," he said. He also pointed to suppliers from the Western Hemisphere, including the United States and Canada, as potential sources to fill the Hormuz gap.

The government has also moved on the export side. Last week, the Centre reduced special additional excise duties on petrol, diesel, and aviation turbine fuel exports — cutting petrol export duty by 50 percent and ATF export duty by 40 percent — to keep Indian refiners competitive while managing the domestic supply balance.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora, the fuel price trajectory has cascading implications. Higher energy costs feed directly into food inflation, logistics costs, and the price of every good that moves by road in India — which is to say, nearly everything. Remittances sent home buy less when the rupee is weakening and inflation is rising.

The Indian foreign ministry, separately on Monday, expressed "utmost concern" over renewed hostilities between Iran and Israel, calling on all parties to immediately de-escalate and conclude ongoing negotiations. The diplomatic language was unusually direct.

Puri's message was calibrated to project control: reserves are adequate, alternatives are flowing, prices will fall. But the caveat he himself offered — that a prolonged conflict means "global depression" — suggests the government's confidence is conditional on a war that ends sooner rather than later. That outcome is not in India's hands.
